name: Fennel
preparation_as_written: The text describes boiling the seed in water or wine and taking the resulting liquor; the seeds were also chewed after meals.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that fennel eases wind and gripings of the belly, helps a queasy stomach, and provokes the appetite.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary herb. Eating or drinking fennel at food-strength amounts is not associated with significant risk for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Limited modern evidence supports fennel as a carminative for mild bloating and infant colic; effects are modest and studies are small.

name: Mint (Peppermint and Spearmint)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Mentha species; Culpeper's 'mint' covers several, closest to modern spearmint (Mentha spicata) and peppermint (Mentha x piperita)

preparation_as_written: The text describes mint taken as a hot infusion in water, or the juice taken, to settle the stomach.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that mint stays the stomach, stops vomiting, and is good against wind and the gripings of the belly.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary and tea herb. Food- and tea-strength use is well tolerated by most people; concentrated peppermint oil is a different, stronger preparation and can worsen reflux in some people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Peppermint (notably enteric-coated oil) has reasonable modern evidence for irritable bowel symptoms; ordinary mint tea has weaker but supportive evidence for mild indigestion.

name: Chamomile

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Chamaemelum nobile (Roman chamomile); modern teas often use Matricaria chamomilla (German chamomile)

preparation_as_written: The text describes the flowers infused in water as a warm drink, and also boiled to make a bath or fomentation applied to the body.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that chamomile eases pains of the belly and colic, comforts the stomach, and that a bath of it eases weariness and pains.

modern_caution.notes: Widely used as a mild tea. Generally well tolerated; people with severe allergy to plants in the daisy/ragweed family may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Modest modern evidence for mild calming and digestive-comfort effects; evidence is limited and mostly low-quality.

name: Centaury

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Centaurium erythraea (common centaury); not to be confused with the unrelated garden plant Centaurea

preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the bitter decoction drunk.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that this bitter herb helps a weak stomach, opens obstructions of the liver, and provokes appetite.

modern_caution.notes: A bitter tonic herb. Generally low-risk at traditional amounts, but bitters can aggravate stomach ulcers or excess acid, and concentrated use is not well studied. Caution in pregnancy due to lack of safety data.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Used in traditional bitter formulas; little rigorous modern clinical evidence for the historical claims.

name: Wormwood
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb steeped in wine or ale, or boiled in water, and the bitter liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that wormwood strengthens a weak stomach, helps digestion, kills worms in the belly, and opens obstructions of the liver.

modern_caution.notes: Wormwood contains thujone, a compound that is toxic to the nervous system and can cause seizures and kidney damage at higher or prolonged doses. It should not be used in pregnancy and is not safe for self-directed internal use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Standardised thujone-free extracts are studied for some digestive and inflammatory conditions, but the traditional whole-herb internal preparation described here carries real toxicity risk and is not a recommended modern treatment.

name: Aloes (Bitter Aloes)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Dried latex of Aloe species (bitter aloes / aloe resin) — distinct from the clear aloe vera gel sold today

preparation_as_written: The text describes the bitter dried resin taken in small quantity to purge the belly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that aloes purge the belly of choler and phlegm and open the body when it is bound (constipated).

modern_caution.notes: Bitter aloes is a powerful stimulant purgative. It can cause severe cramping, fluid and electrolyte loss, and is unsafe in pregnancy (risk of uterine stimulation) and for children. Repeated use can damage bowel function. The historical 'aloes' here is not the same as the clear aloe vera gel sold for skin.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Aloe latex is recognised as a strong laxative but is not recommended in modern practice because of its toxicity and safety concerns; safer alternatives exist.

name: Senna

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes the leaves infused in water, sometimes with ginger or aniseed added to lessen griping, and the liquor taken to loosen the body.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents senna as a purge to loosen the belly and carry off 'gross humours'.

modern_caution.notes: Senna is still used today as a stimulant laxative, but it is not for routine or long-term use, can cause cramping and fluid loss, and is generally avoided in pregnancy and in young children except under professional guidance.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Senna has good modern evidence as a short-term stimulant laxative and is an approved over-the-counter medicine in many countries, with the cautions noted above.

name: Marigold (Calendula)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Calendula officinalis (pot marigold) — not the unrelated ornamental Tagetes 'marigold'

preparation_as_written: The text describes the flowers made into an ointment or the juice applied, and also the flowers used in broths.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that marigold strengthens the heart, and that an ointment of the flowers is used for inflammations of the skin and to help heal wounds.

modern_caution.notes: Calendula is commonly used in modern skin balms and is generally well tolerated on intact skin; people allergic to the daisy family may react. Topical use only is implied here.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some modest modern evidence supports topical calendula for minor skin irritation and wound soothing; quality of evidence is limited.

name: Plantain (Ribwort / Greater Plantain)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Plantago major or Plantago lanceolata (broadleaf / ribwort plantain) — not the banana-like 'plantain' food

preparation_as_written: The text describes the bruised leaves laid on the skin, and the juice applied to sores.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that plantain cools and heals, is good for sores and wounds, and for the bites and stings of creatures.

modern_caution.notes: Plantain leaf applied to skin is a mild traditional remedy with no known significant risk for most people on minor, clean skin irritation.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; limited laboratory and small-study evidence for soothing and mild wound-supporting effects.

name: Houseleek
preparation_as_written: The text describes the cool, juicy leaves bruised and laid on the skin, or the juice applied.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that houseleek cools hot inflammations, eases the heat of burns and St. Anthony's fire, and is laid on hot swellings.

modern_caution.notes: Used much like aloe vera gel — the cool leaf juice applied to intact skin. Low risk for most people; not a substitute for proper burn care on anything beyond very minor burns.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little formal modern clinical evidence, though the cooling, moisture-rich leaf is plausibly soothing on minor irritation.

name: Comfrey
preparation_as_written: The text describes the slimy root boiled and made into a poultice or drink, and used both on the skin and taken inwardly for inward hurts.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that comfrey heals wounds and broken bones, knits together what is broken, and is taken inwardly for inward wounds and bruises.

modern_caution.notes: Comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can cause serious liver damage. Taking it internally (as the historical text also describes) is now considered unsafe. Even on the skin, modern guidance restricts it to short-term use on intact (unbroken) skin only, and it should not be used in pregnancy or on children.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Topical comfrey preparations have some modern evidence for short-term relief of bruises, sprains and joint pain, but internal use is regarded as unsafe and is banned or restricted in several countries.

name: Greater Celandine

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Chelidonium majus (greater celandine) — unrelated to lesser celandine, Ficaria verna

preparation_as_written: The text describes the bright yellow-orange juice of the broken stem dabbed onto the skin, and the herb also taken inwardly in decoctions.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that the juice cleanses the skin, takes away warts, tetters and spots, and is used for sore eyes and for the yellow jaundice.

modern_caution.notes: Greater celandine taken internally has been linked to serious, sometimes severe liver injury (hepatotoxicity), and the fresh juice is irritating to skin and eyes. The historical eye and internal uses are unsafe; it should not be used in pregnancy or by children.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Topical use on warts has weak traditional support, but internal preparations are associated with documented cases of acute liver injury and are not recommended.

name: Elder

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes elder flowers made into a water or ointment for the skin, and the berries and inner bark prepared into purging and 'cleansing' preparations.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents elder flower preparations for the complexion and skin, and stronger bark and berry preparations to purge and cleanse the body.

modern_caution.notes: Elderflower and properly cooked elderberry are widely used and generally low-risk. However, the raw berries, leaves, bark and unripe fruit contain cyanide-producing compounds and can cause nausea and vomiting; the purging bark preparations described historically are the risky ones. Identify the part used carefully.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Cooked elderberry has some modern evidence for shortening cold and flu symptoms; the historical purging bark/raw-berry uses are not recommended due to toxicity of the raw plant.

name: White Horehound
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water with honey and the syrup taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that horehound helps to expel tough phlegm from the chest, eases an old cough, and helps those who are short of breath.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional cough herb, still found in horehound cough sweets. Food- and sweet-strength use is low-risk for most people; very large amounts can upset the stomach. Best avoided in pregnancy due to limited data.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional use for cough and as a bitter; modern clinical evidence is limited and mostly low-quality.

name: Hyssop
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled with honey or figs and the liquor or syrup taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that hyssop helps coughs, shortness of breath, and brings up tough phlegm from the lungs.

modern_caution.notes: Culinary-strength hyssop herb and tea are low-risk for most people. Note that concentrated hyssop essential oil is a separate, much stronger product that can cause seizures and should not be used internally — the herb described here is not that oil.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use for coughs and colds; little rigorous modern clinical evidence.

name: Elecampane
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root boiled or candied (preserved in sugar) and taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that elecampane root helps the cough, shortness of breath and wheezing of the lungs, and helps to bring up phlegm.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional cough root. Generally low-risk at traditional amounts, though it can occasionally cause skin allergy on contact, and large amounts may upset the stomach. Limited data in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; some laboratory evidence for antimicrobial and expectorant activity, but little modern clinical trial evidence.

name: Mullein
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves and flowers boiled in water and the liquor taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that mullein is good for coughs and to ease the chest, and that a decoction is used for hoarseness.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional cough herb, generally low-risk as a tea for most people. The fine hairs on the leaf can irritate the throat, so traditional preparations are strained well.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; limited laboratory evidence for soothing and antimicrobial effects and little modern clinical trial data.

name: Coltsfoot
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves boiled in water and the liquor taken, and the dried leaves sometimes smoked, for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that coltsfoot is good for the cough and for shortness of breath, and helps the 'rheum' that falls upon the lungs.

modern_caution.notes: Coltsfoot contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can cause serious liver damage, especially with repeated use. Internal use is now considered unsafe; it should not be used in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, or by children. Some countries restrict its sale.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional cough use only; the liver-toxicity risk from its pyrrolizidine alkaloids means internal use is not recommended in modern practice, and pyrrolizidine-free cultivars are not reliably available to the public.

name: Liquorice

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes the root boiled in water, often with other chest herbs, and the sweet liquor taken for coughs and a sore chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents liquorice for coughs, hoarseness, and to soothe a raw or sore chest and throat.

modern_caution.notes: Liquorice root soothes the throat but, taken in quantity or over time, can raise blood pressure, lower potassium, and cause fluid retention. It is contraindicated for people with high blood pressure, heart or kidney problems, in pregnancy, and can interact with several medicines including some blood-pressure and heart drugs.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Liquorice and its derivatives have some modern evidence for soothing coughs and for digestive uses, but the blood-pressure and potassium effects are well documented and limit safe amounts.

name: Pennyroyal
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb boiled in water or wine and the liquor taken, and notes its use to 'provoke the courses' (bring on menstruation).
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that pennyroyal provokes women's courses, expels the dead child and afterbirth, helps wind and gripings of the belly, and is used for coughs.

modern_caution.notes: Pennyroyal — and especially its concentrated oil — is acutely poisonous. It has caused fatal liver and kidney failure, and its historical use to bring on menstruation or end pregnancy has killed people attempting it. There is no safe self-directed dose for these purposes. If you are pregnant, think you may be, or have a missed or worrying period, this is a situation for a healthcare professional, not a historical remedy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No legitimate modern use supports internal pennyroyal for these purposes; poison-control and medical literature document severe and fatal toxicity, including deaths from attempted self-induced abortion.

name: Henbane
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb and its juice or seeds applied outwardly, and warns even within the period that it is dangerous taken inwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that henbane is used to cool hot inflammations and swellings, to ease pain, and to bring sleep — while cautioning against its inward use.

modern_caution.notes: Henbane is a deadly poisonous plant. It contains tropane alkaloids (the same family as deadly nightshade) that can cause delirium, rapid heartbeat, seizures, coma and death, and poisoning has occurred even from skin and mucous-membrane contact. There is no safe home use of this plant.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Purified alkaloids from this plant family are used as tightly controlled prescription medicines, but the raw plant has no safe home use and is documented in poisoning fatalities.

name: Deadly Nightshade
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes outward application of the cooling juice or distilled water to inflamed skin, alongside explicit warnings about the plant's deadly nature.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents it for cooling hot inflammations and swellings of the skin, while stressing that it is poisonous and not to be taken inwardly.

modern_caution.notes: Deadly nightshade is one of the most poisonous plants in Europe. Eating even a few berries can kill a child, and its tropane alkaloids are absorbed through skin and eyes. There is no safe home use. It is listed here only because it appears in the historical source, not as anything to try.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Purified belladonna alkaloids (such as atropine) are important prescription medicines under strict medical control, but the raw plant is a documented cause of serious and fatal poisoning and has no safe home use.

name: Aniseed
preparation_as_written: The text describes the seeds chewed, or boiled in water and the liquor taken, after meals.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that aniseed helps wind and the gripings of the belly, eases the stomach, and helps a stinking breath.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary spice. Seed- and tea-strength use is low-risk for most people; concentrated anise oil is a separate, stronger product.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional carminative use with some small-study support for mild bloating; concentrated extracts are less well studied for safety.

name: Caraway

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes the seeds taken after meals or baked into bread and cakes to settle the stomach.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents caraway to comfort the stomach, help digestion and break wind.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary spice, low-risk at food strength for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Caraway oil (often combined with peppermint) has some modern evidence for indigestion; the whole seed has weaker but supportive traditional use.

name: Angelica

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Angelica archangelica (garden angelica); note wild relatives can be confused with poison hemlock

preparation_as_written: The text describes the root and seeds boiled in wine or water, and the candied stalks eaten, as a warming stomach remedy.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that angelica warms and comforts a cold stomach, helps digestion, eases wind, and was used against infection in plague time.

modern_caution.notes: Angelica contains furocoumarins that can make skin more sensitive to sunlight, and it has a traditional reputation for stimulating menstruation, so it is generally avoided in pregnancy. Foragers must not confuse it with deadly poison hemlock, which it superficially resembles.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional digestive use; limited modern clinical evidence, with the photosensitivity and pregnancy cautions noted above.

name: Gentian (Felwort)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Gentiana lutea (yellow gentian) and related Gentiana species

preparation_as_written: The text describes the bitter root boiled or steeped and the liquor taken to strengthen the stomach.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that gentian, being very bitter, comforts a weak stomach, helps digestion, opens obstructions of the liver, and kills worms.

modern_caution.notes: A strong bitter tonic. Generally low-risk at traditional amounts, but bitters can aggravate stomach ulcers, heartburn or excess acid, and it is usually avoided in pregnancy and with active gastric ulcers.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Used in modern bitter tonics and aperitifs; some evidence for stimulating appetite and digestion, but rigorous clinical data is limited.

name: Rhubarb (Medicinal Rhubarb Root)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Rheum officinale / Rheum palmatum root — the medicinal rhubarbs, not the garden rhubarb grown for its stalks

preparation_as_written: The text describes the dried root powdered or infused and taken in small quantity to purge the belly gently.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that rhubarb root purges choler and phlegm gently, opens the body when it is bound, and afterwards binds and strengthens the stomach.

modern_caution.notes: Medicinal rhubarb root is a stimulant laxative and is not for routine or long-term use; it can cause cramping and fluid loss, is generally avoided in pregnancy and young children, and should be avoided by people with bowel obstruction or kidney stones (it is high in oxalate). The leaves of any rhubarb are toxic and must never be used.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Recognised laxative action with the same cautions as other stimulant laxatives; used in some traditional medicine systems, but safer options are generally preferred.

name: Rue (Herb of Grace)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and notes its use to 'bring down the courses' (provoke menstruation).
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that rue helps wind and gripings, provokes women's courses, and was used against poisons and the bites of venomous creatures.

modern_caution.notes: Rue is a uterine stimulant historically used to bring on menstruation or end pregnancy; in the amounts needed for that it is toxic and has caused serious poisoning, liver and kidney damage, and deaths in attempted self-abortion. The fresh plant also causes severe sun-triggered skin burns on contact. It must not be used in pregnancy or for self-directed internal use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe modern internal use is recommended; the medical and poison-control literature documents toxicity and harm, including from attempted self-induced abortion.

name: Saffron
preparation_as_written: The text describes a few threads steeped in liquid and taken, or added to cordials, in very small quantity.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that saffron strengthens the heart and stomach, helps digestion, and that it cheers the spirits — while cautioning that too much is harmful.

modern_caution.notes: Culinary pinches of saffron are low-risk, but larger medicinal doses are toxic — historically large amounts were used to attempt abortion and have caused poisoning. It is avoided in pregnancy at more than food amounts. Even Culpeper warned against excess.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some modern trials explore saffron for low mood at controlled doses, but higher amounts are toxic and the pregnancy caution is well established.

name: Burdock
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves applied to the skin, and the root and seed boiled and the decoction taken or applied.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that burdock leaves are laid on sores and inflammations, and that the root and seed were used to cleanse the blood and for skin eruptions.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional skin and 'blood-cleansing' herb, low-risk for most people on minor skin complaints. People allergic to the daisy family may react. Note that wild-collected root has occasionally been contaminated with toxic belladonna root, so source matters.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; limited laboratory and small-study evidence for skin and anti-inflammatory effects.

name: Self-Heal
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb bruised and applied, and boiled to make a wash or drink for wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that self-heal is good for wounds inward and outward, for sores in the mouth and throat, and to stay bleeding.

modern_caution.notes: A gentle traditional wound and mouth-rinse herb, low-risk for most people on minor complaints.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; some laboratory evidence for antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity, little modern clinical trial data.

name: Yarrow
preparation_as_written: The text describes the bruised herb applied to wounds to stop bleeding, and an infusion taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that yarrow stanches bleeding, closes and heals wounds, and that a decoction is good for inflammations.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional wound herb, low-risk for most people applied to minor, clean wounds. People allergic to the daisy family may react, and it is generally avoided in pregnancy at medicinal (tea) strength.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; some laboratory support for wound and anti-inflammatory effects, limited clinical evidence.

name: St John's Wort
preparation_as_written: The text describes the flowers steeped in oil to make a red oil for the skin, and the herb boiled and taken inwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that the oil of St John's wort heals wounds, burns and bruises, and that the herb was taken for hurts and melancholy.

modern_caution.notes: Taken internally, St John's wort has serious, well-documented interactions with many medicines — it can make the contraceptive pill, blood thinners, some heart and HIV drugs, transplant medicines and antidepressants stop working properly, sometimes dangerously. It can also increase sensitivity to sunlight. The skin oil is lower-risk, but internal self-use is hazardous if you take any other medication.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: There is reasonable modern evidence for standardised oral extracts in mild-to-moderate low mood, but the drug-interaction risk is significant enough that it should only be used with professional advice.

name: Hemlock
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes only outward application of the cooling herb to inflamed swellings, alongside explicit warnings that it is deadly poison and not to be taken inwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents hemlock applied outwardly to cool hot, painful swellings and inflammations, while stressing its deadly nature.

modern_caution.notes: Hemlock is one of the deadliest plants there is — the poison that killed Socrates. Its alkaloids cause progressive paralysis and death by suffocation, and it is dangerous even handled or absorbed through the skin. It is also lethally easy to mistake for edible plants like wild carrot or parsley. There is no safe home use whatsoever.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No legitimate modern home use exists; the plant is a documented cause of fatal poisoning in humans and livestock.

name: Foxglove
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes an ointment of the bruised herb used outwardly for scabby, scrofulous skin; the powerful effect of the plant on the heart was not understood in Culpeper's time.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents foxglove mainly as an outward ointment for the 'King's evil' (scrofula) and scabby skin conditions.

modern_caution.notes: Foxglove contains powerful heart-affecting compounds (cardiac glycosides). Eating any part can cause a dangerously irregular heartbeat, vomiting and death, and the gap between a 'dose' and a lethal amount is very small. Poisonings happen when the leaves are mistaken for comfrey or other plants. There is no safe home use; the heart drug derived from it (digoxin) requires careful medical dosing and monitoring.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Purified, precisely dosed digitalis derivatives are genuine prescription heart medicines, but the raw plant is a documented cause of fatal poisoning and has no safe home use.

name: Honey

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes honey mixed into warm drinks and electuaries with herbs such as horehound or hyssop, and applied to sores.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents honey to soothe a sore throat and cough, as a base for chest medicines, and applied to wounds and sores.

modern_caution.notes: Honey is low-risk and soothing for most people. The one firm exception: never give honey to a baby under 12 months old, because of the risk of infant botulism.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Honey has reasonable modern evidence for easing cough and sore throat in adults and older children, and medical-grade honey is used on some wounds.

name: Thyme
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water with honey and the liquor taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that thyme helps a cough and shortness of breath, brings up phlegm, and comforts the stomach.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary herb. Tea- and food-strength thyme is low-risk for most people; concentrated thyme essential oil is a separate, much stronger product that should not be swallowed undiluted.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Thyme preparations have some modern evidence as part of cough remedies (often with ivy); the everyday herb tea has weaker but supportive traditional use.

name: Lungwort

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Pulmonaria officinalis (lungwort); historically the name was also used for a tree lichen, Lobaria pulmonaria

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves boiled in water and the liquor taken for the lungs.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that lungwort is good for the diseases of the lungs, for coughs, wheezing and shortness of breath.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional lung herb, generally low-risk as a tea for most people. Note the historical name covers more than one plant, so identity in old recipes can be uncertain.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional ('doctrine of signatures') use; little modern clinical evidence for the lung claims.

name: Garlic
preparation_as_written: The text describes garlic eaten, boiled into a posset, or applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that garlic helps cold coughs and shortness of breath, expels wind, and was used against infection and the bites of venomous creatures — while noting it is too hot for choleric or feverish people.

modern_caution.notes: Culinary garlic is low-risk, but in larger medicinal amounts garlic thins the blood and can add to the effect of blood-thinning medicines and increase bleeding risk around surgery. Applying raw garlic directly to skin can cause chemical burns.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Garlic has modest modern evidence for small effects on blood pressure and cholesterol; the historical cough/infection uses are mostly traditional. The blood-thinning interaction is well documented.

name: White Poppy (Opium Poppy)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Papaver somniferum (opium poppy) — the source of opium

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes a syrup or decoction made from the poppy heads, taken to cause sleep and quiet a cough — a preparation now understood to contain opium.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents poppy preparations to procure sleep, ease pain, and quiet violent coughs and 'rheums'.

modern_caution.notes: The white poppy is the opium poppy. Home preparations of the heads contain opium alkaloids (including morphine and codeine) in unknown, uncontrolled strengths, which can dangerously slow or stop breathing — especially in children, where poppy-head preparations have caused deaths. There is no safe way to self-dose this at home, and it is controlled by law in many places.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Purified, precisely dosed opioid medicines derived from this plant are essential prescription drugs under strict control, but uncontrolled home preparations are dangerous and historically lethal, particularly for infants.

name: Tobacco
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb made into ointments and poultices for the skin, the smoke drawn for the chest, and the juice used — uses now understood to deliver toxic nicotine.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents tobacco for the chest and to bring up phlegm, and outwardly in ointments for old sores, swellings and skin complaints.

modern_caution.notes: Tobacco contains nicotine, which is highly poisonous — it can be absorbed through skin and through broken skin from poultices, causing nausea, a racing or irregular heartbeat, collapse and, in concentrated form, death. Children are especially vulnerable. Beyond acute poisoning, smoking it carries the well-known long-term cancer and heart-and-lung risks.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe modern home medicinal use; nicotine poisoning from skin contact is documented, and tobacco's long-term harms are among the best-established in medicine.

name: Rosemary

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes rosemary boiled in water or wine, the steam breathed in, and the herb worn or burned, for the head and chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents rosemary to comfort the head and memory, to help colds and the chest, and as a fragrant strewing and washing herb.

modern_caution.notes: Culinary- and tea-strength rosemary is low-risk for most people. Concentrated rosemary essential oil is a separate, much stronger product that should not be swallowed; very large medicinal amounts of the herb are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional and culinary use; limited modern evidence, mainly small studies on aroma and alertness.

name: Sage

source.title: A Book of Simples
source.author: transcribed by Henry William Lewer (manuscript c.1600s, published 1908)

preparation_as_written: The manuscript describes sage boiled in water and used as a warm gargle and drink for the mouth and throat.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: The text presents sage as a gargle for a sore mouth and throat, to help the head, and to comfort the body.

modern_caution.notes: A sage gargle or culinary use is low-risk, but sage contains thujone, so strong sage tea taken in quantity over time, and especially sage essential oil, can be harmful and (in oil form) trigger seizures. Medicinal-strength internal use is avoided in pregnancy and while breastfeeding (it can reduce milk supply).
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Sage gargles/sprays have some modern evidence for sore throat; the thujone caution applies to strong or prolonged internal use and to the essential oil.

name: Balm (Lemon Balm)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves infused in water or wine and the warm drink taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that balm comforts the heart and stomach, drives away melancholy, and helps digestion and wind.

modern_caution.notes: A mild culinary and tea herb, low-risk for most people at tea strength.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some modest modern evidence for mild calming effects and for digestive comfort; studies are small.

name: Dill
preparation_as_written: The text describes the seed boiled in water and the liquor taken, and the herb eaten.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that dill stays the belly from wind and gripings, eases the stomach, and stops hiccups.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary herb, low-risk at food and tea strength for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional carminative; 'dill water' has long folk use for infant wind, but rigorous modern evidence is limited.

name: Barberry
preparation_as_written: The text describes the bark and berries boiled, and the sharp berries used in conserves, the liquor taken for the stomach and liver.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that barberry cools a hot stomach and liver, helps a yellow complexion (jaundice), and stays looseness and heat in the body.

modern_caution.notes: Barberry contains berberine. Small culinary amounts of the berry are low-risk, but medicinal doses of the bark/root can upset the stomach, lower blood sugar and blood pressure, and berberine interacts with several medicines. It is avoided in pregnancy because it can stimulate the uterus.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Berberine (the active compound) has some modern evidence for blood sugar and cholesterol, but with real interaction and pregnancy cautions; the whole-herb historical uses are less studied.

name: Chickweed
preparation_as_written: The text describes the bruised herb laid on the skin and boiled into an ointment.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that chickweed cools hot, red swellings and itching, and an ointment of it helps sores and inflammations.

modern_caution.notes: A mild cooling skin herb, low-risk applied to minor irritation for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional use; little formal modern evidence, though it is a common ingredient in soothing skin balms.

name: Solomon's Seal
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root bruised and applied as a poultice, and the distilled water used on the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that Solomon's seal closes and heals wounds, and that it is famous for taking away bruises and the marks of blows and falls.

modern_caution.notes: Traditionally used on the skin for bruises; low-risk topically for most people on minor injuries. The raw berries are not for eating.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Sanicle
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and used as a wash and drink for wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that sanicle heals green wounds and ulcers, inward and outward, and stays bleeding.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional wound herb, low-risk for most people on minor, clean wounds.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; limited modern evidence.

name: Cleavers (Goosegrass)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the juice taken and the herb boiled, used inwardly and on the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that cleavers cleanses the blood and skin, helps scabby eruptions, and the juice was used for the complexion.

modern_caution.notes: A mild traditional skin and lymphatic herb, low-risk for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional 'blood-cleansing' use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Walnut
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves and green outer husks boiled and used as a wash, and the kernels eaten.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that the leaves and husks are used to cleanse the skin of scabs and spreading sores, and against worms.

modern_caution.notes: Walnut leaf/husk washes are low-risk on intact skin for most people; the husk stains skin strongly. People with tree-nut allergy should be cautious.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; some laboratory evidence for astringent and antimicrobial activity of the leaf.

name: Cucumber
preparation_as_written: The text describes the cool pulp and juice laid on the face and skin, and the seeds used in cooling drinks.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that cucumber cools hot, inflamed and sunburnt skin and helps a red, pimpled face.

modern_caution.notes: A food, low-risk applied to the skin or eaten for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Cooling effect is real but largely from moisture; little specific modern medical evidence beyond soothing.

name: Dock (Yellow Dock)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Rumex species, especially Rumex crispus (yellow/curled dock)

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves laid on the skin (famously rubbed on nettle stings), and the root boiled and taken inwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that dock leaves ease nettle stings and that the root cleanses the blood, helps scabby skin (the itch), and gently loosens the belly.

modern_caution.notes: Leaf used on the skin is low-risk, but the root is a mild laxative and dock is high in oxalates; large or prolonged amounts are best avoided, especially by people prone to kidney stones, and it is generally avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional 'alterative' and mild laxative use; limited modern clinical evidence.

name: Marsh Mallow
preparation_as_written: The text describes the slimy root and leaves boiled to a soothing drink, and made into a poultice for the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that marshmallow softens and soothes, eases a cough and rough throat, and that a poultice eases hard swellings and inflammations.

modern_caution.notes: A gentle soothing (demulcent) herb, low-risk for most people. Because its mucilage can coat the gut, it is sensibly taken apart in time from other medicines so it does not slow their absorption.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some modern evidence for soothing dry cough and throat irritation via its mucilage; well regarded as a demulcent.

name: Maidenhair

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Adiantum capillus-veneris (maidenhair fern); the name was also used for related ferns

preparation_as_written: The text describes the fern boiled in water, often made into a syrup with sugar, and taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that maidenhair helps coughs, shortness of breath, and brings up phlegm from the chest.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional cough fern, generally low-risk as a tea/syrup for most people. The historical name covered several ferns, so identity in old recipes can be uncertain.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Ground Ivy (Alehoof)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water, formerly used to clear ale, and the liquor taken for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that ground ivy helps a cough and the diseases of the lungs, and clears tough phlegm.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional chest herb, low-risk as a tea for most people; large medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; limited modern evidence.

name: Wood Sorrel
preparation_as_written: The text describes the sharp, sour leaves made into a cooling drink or 'green sauce'.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that wood sorrel cools a hot, feverish stomach, quenches thirst in fevers, and strengthens a weak stomach against vomiting.

modern_caution.notes: A sharp, sorrel-like leaf, fine in small culinary amounts. Like other sorrels it is high in oxalic acid, so large quantities are best avoided, especially by people prone to kidney stones.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional cooling/thirst use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Feverfew
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and taken, and applied outwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that feverfew is good for pains in the head, helps agues (fevers), and was used for women's complaints.

modern_caution.notes: Best known today for migraine. It can cause mouth ulcers and irritation when the fresh leaf is chewed, and stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause rebound headaches. It can add to blood-thinning medicines, the daisy-allergic may react, and it is avoided in pregnancy (it can stimulate the uterus).
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: There is some modern evidence for standardised feverfew in preventing migraine; the cautions above are well recognised.

name: Meadowsweet
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb and flowers boiled in water or wine and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that meadowsweet helps agues (fevers), eases pains, and comforts the stomach and a looseness of the belly.

modern_caution.notes: Meadowsweet naturally contains salicylates — the aspirin-like compounds. For that reason it carries aspirin's cautions: it should not be given to children or teenagers (risk of Reye's syndrome), and is avoided by people with aspirin/salicylate allergy, asthma triggered by aspirin, ulcers, or on blood thinners.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional use for fever, pain and stomach upset is consistent with its salicylate content, but it carries the same risks as aspirin and lacks controlled dosing.

name: Willow Bark
preparation_as_written: The text describes the bark and leaves boiled in water and the liquor taken, and applied outwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that willow cools heat and fevers, stays bleeding, and that the bark was used to ease pains and inflammations.

modern_caution.notes: Willow bark is the original natural source of the aspirin-like salicylates. It therefore carries aspirin's cautions: not for children or teenagers (Reye's syndrome risk), and avoided by people with salicylate/aspirin allergy, ulcers, asthma triggered by aspirin, or taking blood thinners. Home preparations have an unknown, variable strength.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Standardised willow-bark extracts have some modern evidence for low-back and joint pain, but with the same risk profile as aspirin and without reliable home dosing.

name: Blessed Thistle
preparation_as_written: The text describes the very bitter herb boiled and the liquor taken, and used in plague time as a sweating, strengthening drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that blessed thistle strengthens the stomach and helps digestion, provokes sweat in fevers, and was esteemed against infection and the plague.

modern_caution.notes: A strong bitter. Small amounts stimulate appetite, but larger doses can cause vomiting. It is avoided in pregnancy, and people allergic to the daisy family may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional bitter and 'sweating' herb; little rigorous modern clinical evidence, and large doses are deliberately emetic.

name: Valerian
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root boiled or steeped and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that valerian was used to ease pains, to help those troubled in sleep, and against the trembling and shaking of the body.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional sedative herb. It is generally mild, but it can add to the drowsiness of alcohol, sleeping tablets, sedatives and some painkillers, so it should not be combined with them or taken before driving. Safety in pregnancy is not established.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mixed modern evidence for mild improvement in sleep; the interaction with other sedatives is the main practical caution.

name: Wood Betony

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Betonica officinalis (wood betony), formerly Stachys officinalis

preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water or wine and the liquor taken, and the powder snuffed.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that betony is good for pains and aches of the head, comforts the stomach, and was greatly esteemed as a general strengthening herb.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional tea herb, low-risk for most people at tea strength; large medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Vervain
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and applied outwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that vervain helps headaches and the pains of the head, eases nervous complaints, and was used for many disorders.

modern_caution.notes: Generally mild, but vervain has a traditional reputation for stimulating the uterus and is therefore avoided in pregnancy. It may also mildly affect blood pressure.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; little modern clinical evidence, with the pregnancy caution widely repeated.

name: Lavender
preparation_as_written: The text describes the flowers infused, the distilled water used, and the herb worn and smelled.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that lavender comforts the head and brain, eases the pains and griefs of the head, and was used for faintness and low spirits.

modern_caution.notes: Lavender as a tea, dried flowers or aroma is low-risk for most people. Concentrated lavender essential oil is a separate, much stronger product that should not be swallowed.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some modern evidence for mild anxiety relief (including a standardised oral capsule); aroma effects are modest.

name: Hops
preparation_as_written: The text describes the young shoots eaten and the flowers boiled, the liquor taken to cleanse the blood.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that hops open obstructions of the liver and spleen, cleanse the blood, and help a feverish heat; hops were also long valued to ease rest and sleep.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional sleep and bitter herb, low-risk for most people; it can add mildly to the drowsiness of sedatives. Pickers sometimes get a skin rash from the fresh plant.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some traditional and limited modern support for mild sedative effects, often combined with valerian.

name: Cowslip
preparation_as_written: The text describes the flowers made into a wine or syrup, and the distilled water used.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that cowslip flowers ease pains of the head, help those troubled in sleep, and were used to quiet the nerves and for the palsy.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional gentle flower remedy, low-risk for most people. People allergic to primula may get a skin reaction, and it is best avoided in pregnancy and with blood thinners (it contains small amounts of salicylates).
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; little modern clinical evidence for the flowers.

name: Mandrake
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the root used outwardly and notes its dangerous, stupefying power; old surgery used it to dull pain and bring sleep, with great risk.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents mandrake as a cooling, narcotic plant once used to bring deep sleep and deaden pain, while stressing that it is dangerous and not to be meddled with.

modern_caution.notes: Mandrake contains the same deadly tropane alkaloids as deadly nightshade and henbane. It can cause delirium, a racing heart, breathing failure, coma and death, and the gap between a sleep-inducing amount and a lethal one is dangerously small. There is no safe home use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Of historical interest as an early anaesthetic, but it has no safe home use today and is a documented cause of serious poisoning.

name: Tansy
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb boiled or beaten into 'tansies' (cakes), and notes its use to 'bring down the courses' (provoke menstruation) and against worms.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents tansy to provoke women's courses, to expel worms, and to ease gripings of the belly.

modern_caution.notes: Tansy contains thujone and is toxic in the amounts historically used to bring on menstruation or end pregnancy. It can cause vomiting, seizures, organ damage and has caused deaths, including in attempted self-abortion. It must not be used in pregnancy or for self-directed internal use, and the oil is especially dangerous.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe modern internal use is recommended; poisoning and fatalities, including from attempted abortion, are documented.

name: Mugwort
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and notes its long use to 'bring down the courses' and ease women's complaints.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents mugwort to provoke women's courses, help the delivery of the afterbirth, and ease cramps and gripings of the belly.

modern_caution.notes: Mugwort is a uterine stimulant traditionally used to bring on menstruation, and it contains thujone. It must not be used in pregnancy, where it carries a miscarriage risk, and self-directed internal use to affect periods is unsafe. It is also a common cause of hay-fever-type and skin allergy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; the uterine-stimulant and pregnancy risks are well recognised, and there is no safe self-directed internal use for the historical menstrual purposes.

name: Motherwort
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor or a conserve taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that motherwort makes a merry, cheerful soul, settles a trembling heart and palpitations, and was used to help women in childbearing.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional heart-calming and women's herb. It is a uterine stimulant and so is avoided in pregnancy, and because it can affect heart rhythm and add to heart and blood-thinning medicines, anyone with heart problems should not self-treat with it.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Limited modern evidence; mostly traditional use, with recognised cautions in pregnancy and for people on heart medication.

name: Savin
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the dried leaves powdered and the herb used, and records its notorious use to 'force the courses' and expel the dead child — a use already known to be highly dangerous.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents savin to provoke women's courses and expel the afterbirth or dead child, and outwardly against worms and skin growths.

modern_caution.notes: Savin was historically one of the most infamous abortion herbs, and one of the most lethal. The amount needed to affect a pregnancy is close to the amount that causes violent poisoning, kidney damage and death; it has killed many women in attempted self-abortion. There is no safe dose for any purpose. A missed period or pregnancy concern is a matter for a healthcare professional, never this plant.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No legitimate modern use; the medical and historical record documents severe poisoning and death, especially from attempted abortion.

name: Birthwort
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the root used to help expel the afterbirth and cleanse the womb, and applied to foul wounds and ulcers.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents birthwort to bring away the afterbirth and 'cleanse' the womb after childbirth, and outwardly to cleanse old sores and ulcers.

modern_caution.notes: Birthwort contains aristolochic acid, which is now confirmed to be a potent cause of cancer and of irreversible kidney failure — large groups of people have suffered kidney destruction and urinary-tract cancer from products containing it. There is no safe amount, and it is banned for medicinal use in many countries. It must never be used.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Modern evidence is decisively negative on safety: aristolochic acid is an established human carcinogen and nephrotoxin, and the plant is prohibited for medicinal use in many jurisdictions.

name: Raspberry Leaf
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves boiled in water and used as a wash and a drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that raspberry leaves are binding and were used as a wash for sores of the mouth and as a strengthening drink for women.

modern_caution.notes: Raspberry leaf tea is generally mild, but because it can act on the uterus it is traditionally reserved for the later weeks of pregnancy and under midwife or medical guidance — not for early pregnancy or for trying to affect a period on your own.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Limited and mixed modern evidence for use in late pregnancy/labour preparation; widely used but not strongly proven.

name: Parsley
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root and seed boiled in water and the liquor taken, and the herb eaten.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that parsley provokes urine, opens obstructions, eases the stone and wind, and 'provokes the courses'.

modern_caution.notes: Eating parsley as a food or garnish is low-risk. But concentrated parsley seed, oil, or large medicinal amounts act strongly on the kidneys and uterus and have historically been used to try to bring on periods or end pregnancy; in those amounts they can harm the kidneys and are unsafe, and are avoided in pregnancy and in kidney disease.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Culinary use is safe and the diuretic effect is real but mild; the concentrated medicinal/abortifacient uses are unsafe and not recommended.

name: Juniper
preparation_as_written: The text describes the berries boiled in water and the liquor taken, and used in strong waters and against wind.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that juniper berries provoke urine, expel wind, help the stone and were thought to strengthen the stomach and resist infection.

modern_caution.notes: A few juniper berries as a culinary flavouring are fine, but in the larger amounts used medicinally, and especially as the oil, juniper irritates the kidneys and stimulates the uterus. It is unsafe for people with kidney disease, should not be used in pregnancy (historical abortifacient use), and prolonged use can damage the kidneys.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Recognised mild diuretic at culinary levels; medicinal/oil doses carry kidney and pregnancy risks and are not recommended.

name: Pellitory of the Wall
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water and the liquor taken, and used as a poultice.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that pellitory provokes urine, eases the stone and a stoppage of water, and that a poultice eases hot swellings.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional mild diuretic herb, low-risk for most people, though it is a notorious hay-fever pollen plant and the allergic may react to handling it.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional diuretic use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Horsetail

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Equisetum arvense (field horsetail); not the toxic marsh horsetail, Equisetum palustre

preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water and the liquor taken, and applied to wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that horsetail stays bleeding, provokes urine, and that it heals wounds and ulcers, inward and outward.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional diuretic and wound herb. It contains an enzyme (thiaminase) that can deplete vitamin B1 with prolonged use, so it is not for long-term use, for children, or for people who drink heavily or are poorly nourished. Correct identification matters — the similar marsh horsetail is toxic.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Limited modern evidence for a mild diuretic effect; the thiaminase and species-identity cautions are well recognised.

name: Nettle
preparation_as_written: The text describes the young tops boiled and eaten or made into a drink, and the juice taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that nettles provoke urine, open obstructions, cleanse the blood, help the chest and were used to stay bleeding.

modern_caution.notes: Cooked nettle (the sting is destroyed by cooking) is a nutritious food. As a medicinal it is a mild diuretic and may add to the effect of blood-pressure, water (diuretic), blood-sugar and blood-thinning medicines, so people on those should be cautious; medicinal-strength use is generally avoided in pregnancy. The fresh plant stings.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some modern evidence for nettle in hay fever and (the root) in benign prostate symptoms; the interaction cautions are sensible.

name: Broom

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Cytisus scoparius (common broom), formerly Sarothamnus scoparius

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the flowers, seed and tops boiled and the liquor taken to purge and provoke urine.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents broom to provoke urine strongly, to purge watery humours (dropsy), and to cleanse the kidneys.

modern_caution.notes: Broom contains sparteine and related compounds that act powerfully on the heart's rhythm and stimulate the uterus. In medicinal amounts it can slow or disturb the heartbeat and is dangerous for people with heart problems or high blood pressure; it must not be used in pregnancy, and it can interact badly with certain medicines (including MAOI antidepressants).
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Its active compound sparteine was once a regulated heart drug, but the whole-herb home use is unsafe and not recommended.

name: Tormentil
preparation_as_written: The text describes the very astringent root boiled in water or wine and used as a wash, gargle and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that tormentil is exceedingly binding, stays all kinds of fluxes (looseness) and bleeding, and fastens loose teeth and gums as a wash.

modern_caution.notes: A strongly astringent (tannin-rich) root, low-risk as an occasional mouth rinse or gargle for most people. Its high tannin content can upset the stomach if a lot is swallowed, and tannins can reduce iron absorption if taken with meals.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional astringent use for looseness and mouth complaints; limited modern clinical evidence.

name: Bistort (Snakeweed)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the astringent root boiled and used as a gargle and wash, and taken inwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that bistort is very binding, stays looseness and bleeding, and that a gargle helps sore mouths, gums and throats.

modern_caution.notes: Another tannin-rich astringent root, low-risk as an occasional gargle or wash for most people; large swallowed amounts of tannins can upset the stomach and reduce iron absorption.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional astringent use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Agrimony
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled in water or wine and used as a gargle and drink, and applied to wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that agrimony is good for the liver, helps sore throats as a gargle, and cleanses and heals wounds.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent herb, low-risk as a tea or gargle for most people. It contains some tannins and a little vitamin K, so people on blood thinners may wish to be consistent; large medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional astringent and gargle use; limited modern clinical evidence.

name: Sloe (Blackthorn)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Prunus spinosa (blackthorn); the fruit, flowers and bark

preparation_as_written: The text describes the sharp unripe fruit and the flowers and bark boiled, the liquor used as a binding gargle and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that sloes are very binding, that the juice stays looseness and bleeding, and a gargle helps a relaxed, sore throat and mouth.

modern_caution.notes: The astringent fruit and flowers are low-risk as an occasional gargle or in conserves for most people. As with related stone fruits, the kernels inside the stones contain cyanide-forming compounds and should not be crushed and eaten.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional astringent use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Hawthorn
preparation_as_written: The text describes the berries and flowers boiled or steeped and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that hawthorn was used to ease an over-stretched or troubled heart and to help the 'dropsy' and stitches in the side.

modern_caution.notes: Hawthorn genuinely acts on the heart and blood vessels, which is exactly why it must be treated with care: it can add to or interfere with heart and blood-pressure medicines (such as digoxin, beta-blockers and others). Heart symptoms — chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, swelling — need proper medical assessment, not self-treatment.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: There is some modern evidence for standardised hawthorn extract as an add-on in heart failure, but only under medical supervision because of its drug interactions.

name: Lily of the Valley

ingredients.historical_name: Lily of the Valley / May Lily

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the flowers distilled into a water and used for the head and heart — a plant now known to powerfully affect the heart.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents lily of the valley water for the head, memory and the heart, and for the palsy.

modern_caution.notes: Every part of lily of the valley contains powerful heart-affecting compounds (cardiac glycosides) much like foxglove. Eating it can cause a dangerously irregular or slow heartbeat, vomiting and death, and children have been poisoned by the berries and even by water the flowers stood in. There is no safe home use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Its glycosides have been used in tightly controlled pharmaceutical settings, but the plant is a documented cause of serious and fatal poisoning and has no safe home use.

name: Borage
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves and flowers put into wine and cordial drinks, and the flowers candied.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that borage cheers the heart, drives away sadness and melancholy, and was used in fevers and cordials to comfort the spirits.

modern_caution.notes: The borage leaf (and to a lesser extent the flowers) contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can damage the liver, particularly with repeated use. For that reason taking the leaf internally is now discouraged. (Borage seed oil, a separate refined product, is treated differently, but the historical leaf-in-wine use is the risky one.)
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: The traditional 'cheering' use is not supported by good evidence, and concern about liver-toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids means internal use of the herb is not recommended.

name: Eyebright
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb made into a water or powder and used for the eyes, as well as taken inwardly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents eyebright, as its name suggests, for the eyes — to help dim or watering eyes and to 'clear the sight'.

modern_caution.notes: The main modern concern is the route: putting any home-made herbal preparation directly into the eye risks infection and injury, because it is not sterile or pH-balanced for the eye. Eye symptoms should be assessed by a pharmacist, optician or doctor rather than self-treated with herbal washes.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Little reliable modern evidence that eyebright helps eye conditions, and applying non-sterile preparations to the eye is specifically discouraged.

name: Avens (Herb Bennet)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the clove-scented root and the herb boiled in water or wine and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that avens comforts and warms a cold, weak stomach, helps digestion, eases gripings, and opens obstructions of the liver.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent, clove-scented herb, low-risk as an occasional tea for most people; large medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional bitter/astringent use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Blackberry (Bramble)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Rubus fruticosus (blackberry/bramble); leaf, root and fruit

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves and root boiled to a binding decoction, used as a drink and a gargle.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that bramble is binding, stays looseness of the belly (the 'flux'), and that a gargle of the leaves fastens loose teeth and helps sore mouths.

modern_caution.notes: The fruit is a food, and a leaf tea is a mild astringent, low-risk for most people; a lot of swallowed tannin can upset the stomach.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional astringent use for mild looseness and mouth complaints; limited modern clinical evidence.

name: Strawberry

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Fragaria vesca (wild strawberry) and cultivated Fragaria species

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves boiled as a wash and drink, and the fruit eaten and the distilled water used.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that strawberry leaves are cooling and binding, good for a hot stomach and looseness, and that a wash of them helps sore mouths and fastens the gums.

modern_caution.notes: Fruit and a mild leaf tea are low-risk for most people; those allergic to strawberries should obviously avoid them.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence for the medicinal claims.

name: Sorrel
preparation_as_written: The text describes the sharp, sour leaves made into a cooling drink or sauce.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that sorrel cools a hot, feverish stomach, quenches thirst, and provokes appetite.

modern_caution.notes: Fine in small culinary amounts, but sorrel is high in oxalic acid; large quantities are best avoided, especially by people prone to kidney stones or with kidney problems.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional cooling/appetite use; the oxalate caution is well recognised, particularly for large amounts.

name: Flax (Linseed)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the seed boiled to a slimy mucilage, taken as a soothing drink and made into a warm poultice for the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that linseed softens and soothes, eases a rough cough and chest, and that a poultice ripens and eases hard swellings and inflammations.

modern_caution.notes: Whole or ground mature linseed is a low-risk gentle bulk laxative — but it must be taken with plenty of fluid, or it can worsen blockage. Large amounts of raw, immature seed are best avoided as they contain trace cyanide-forming compounds.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Linseed has reasonable modern evidence as a bulk-forming laxative and demulcent; the 'take with water' rule is important.

name: Quince
preparation_as_written: The text describes the fruit made into a binding syrup or marmalade, and the slimy seeds soaked to a soothing mucilage.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that quince strengthens a weak stomach, stays vomiting and looseness, and that the seed mucilage soothes a rough tongue and throat.

modern_caution.notes: The cooked fruit is a food and the seed mucilage is soothing, both low-risk for most people. The seeds should be soaked whole, not crushed and eaten, as the kernels contain cyanide-forming compounds.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional astringent/demulcent use; limited modern clinical evidence.

name: Radish
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root eaten and its juice taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that radishes provoke appetite and urine, break wind, and were thought to help bring up phlegm and ease the stone.

modern_caution.notes: A common food, low-risk for most people; large pungent amounts can irritate a sensitive stomach or aggravate reflux.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary/traditional; little specific modern medical evidence.

name: Watercress
preparation_as_written: The text describes the fresh herb eaten and the juice taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that watercress cleanses the blood, provokes appetite and urine, and was esteemed against scurvy.

modern_caution.notes: A nutritious salad leaf, low-risk eaten in normal amounts. Wild watercress from untested water can carry liver-fluke parasites and pollution, so cultivated or thoroughly washed cress is safer.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Recognised as a nutritious, vitamin-C-rich food; the historical 'blood-cleansing' claims are traditional.

name: Common Mallow

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Malva sylvestris (common mallow); a milder relative of marshmallow

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves boiled to a soothing drink and poultice, and used in emollient (softening) ointments.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that mallows soften and ease hot swellings and inflammations, soothe a rough throat and cough, and gently loosen the belly.

modern_caution.notes: A gentle soothing (demulcent) and emollient herb, low-risk for most people on the skin or as a tea.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional demulcent use similar to marshmallow; limited but plausible modern support for soothing effects.

name: Woundwort

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Stachys palustris / Stachys sylvatica (marsh and hedge woundwort)

preparation_as_written: The text describes the bruised herb laid on wounds and boiled into a healing wash and ointment.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that woundwort heals green wounds and cuts, stays bleeding, and that an ointment of it cleanses and closes sores.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional wound herb, low-risk for most people applied to minor, clean wounds.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; limited laboratory evidence for mild antimicrobial activity.

name: Figwort
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled into a wash and ointment and applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that figwort was used for the 'King's evil' (scrofula), for piles, and to cleanse stubborn skin eruptions, sores and swellings.

modern_caution.notes: Used mainly on the skin and traditionally low-risk there. Note it contains compounds that can mildly affect the heart, so internal use is best avoided by people with heart conditions or on heart medication.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional skin use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Oak (Bark and Galls)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the very astringent bark and oak-galls boiled and used as a binding wash, bath, and gargle.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that oak bark is exceedingly binding, stays all fluxes and bleeding, and that a decoction is used as a wash for the skin and a gargle for relaxed throats.

modern_caution.notes: A strong tannin-rich astringent, low-risk for short-term use as a skin wash, bath, or gargle. It should not be used on large broken-skin areas or swallowed in quantity, as a lot of tannin can upset the stomach and reduce iron absorption.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Oak bark is an officially recognised astringent for minor skin inflammation and short-term diarrhoea in some herbal pharmacopoeias, used short term.

name: Fumitory
preparation_as_written: The text describes the juice and a decoction of the herb taken, and the juice applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that fumitory cleanses the blood, helps stubborn skin eruptions, scabs and the itch, and opens obstructions of the liver.

modern_caution.notes: Traditionally used for skin and liver complaints. In larger amounts it can lower blood pressure and affect heart rhythm, and acts as a mild laxative and diuretic, so it is not for prolonged or heavy use and is avoided in pregnancy and with heart or blood-pressure conditions.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some traditional/European use for biliary and skin complaints; modern clinical evidence is limited and dosing matters.

name: Scabious
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken and applied, and the juice used on the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that scabious cleanses the chest of phlegm, and that the juice and an ointment help scabs, itch and stubborn skin sores (hence its name).

modern_caution.notes: A mild traditional skin and chest herb, low-risk for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Periwinkle
preparation_as_written: The text describes the binding leaves bruised and applied, chewed for the mouth, and a decoction taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that periwinkle is binding, stays bleeding (including nosebleeds and bleeding gums), and eases looseness of the belly.

modern_caution.notes: Periwinkle contains active alkaloids; in more than small amounts it can lower blood pressure and is not suitable for people with low blood pressure or who are pregnant. (It is a different plant from the cancer-drug source Madagascar periwinkle, but is still best treated with caution internally.)
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Its alkaloid vincamine has been used in some circulation/memory preparations, but whole-herb home use lacks reliable dosing and carries blood-pressure cautions.

name: Brooklime
preparation_as_written: The text describes the fresh herb eaten as a cress and the juice taken and applied.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that brooklime cleanses the blood, helps stubborn skin eruptions and the scurvy, and provokes urine.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional cress-like 'blood-cleansing' herb, low-risk for most people; like watercress, plants from untested water can carry parasites, so source matters.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Heartsease (Wild Pansy)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that heartsease was used for the chest and for stubborn skin eruptions in children, such as scabs and the 'crusta lactea' (cradle cap/milk crust).

modern_caution.notes: A mild traditional skin herb, low-risk for most people. It contains saponins, so very large amounts taken internally could upset the stomach.
