modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional use for mild eczema/skin complaints; limited modern clinical evidence.

name: Onion
preparation_as_written: The text describes onions eaten, roasted, made into a syrup with honey or sugar, and applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that onions help bring up phlegm and ease the chest, provoke appetite and urine, and that a roasted onion was applied to boils and earache.

modern_caution.notes: A common food, low-risk for most people; raw onion juice on the skin can occasionally irritate, and large amounts can cause heartburn or wind.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary/traditional; the historical cough-syrup use is folk practice with little formal evidence.

name: Horseradish
preparation_as_written: The text describes the pungent root grated and taken, and laid on the skin as a plaster.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that horseradish provokes appetite and urine, helps to bring up phlegm and clear the head and chest, and that a plaster was laid on aching joints.

modern_caution.notes: Small culinary amounts are fine, but the pungent root is a strong irritant: larger amounts can upset the stomach and bowels, and a plaster left on the skin can cause burns and blistering. It is best avoided in stomach ulcers, thyroid problems, and in young children.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some traditional and limited modern use for sinus and urinary complaints (often combined with nasturtium); the irritant cautions are well recognised.

name: Mustard

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Brassica/Sinapis species (black and white mustard) seed

preparation_as_written: The text describes the seed taken in food and made into a paste 'plaster' (a mustard plaster) laid on the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that mustard warms and clears the head and chest, helps bring up phlegm, and that a plaster draws and warms cold, aching parts.

modern_caution.notes: Culinary mustard is fine. The traditional 'mustard plaster', however, is a strong skin irritant that can cause serious chemical burns and blisters if left on too long or used on children or thin skin — it should never be applied directly or for long, and this is the main historical hazard.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mustard plasters/footbaths have long folk use as a counter-irritant for chest and joints; the burn risk is well documented and limits safe use.

name: Pine (Buds and Resin)

ingredients.historical_name: Pine / Fir (the buds, resin and turpentine)
ingredients.modern_equivalent: Pinus species (pine); the young shoots and resin

preparation_as_written: The text describes the young buds and resin boiled to a syrup or the steam inhaled, for the chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that pine buds and resin help the cough and the diseases of the chest, and bring up phlegm.

modern_caution.notes: Pine-bud syrups and steam inhalation are low-risk for most people. Note that purified turpentine oil is a much stronger, toxic product that should not be swallowed — the gentle bud preparation is not that.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Pine-shoot preparations appear in some traditional cough remedies; modern clinical evidence is limited.

name: Marjoram
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb infused and taken, the powder snuffed, and the herb smelled.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that marjoram warms and comforts the head and chest, helps a cold cough and blocked nose, and eases the stomach.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary herb, low-risk at food and tea strength for most people; large medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy, and the concentrated oil is a separate, stronger product.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary/traditional; little formal modern clinical evidence.

name: Savory

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Satureja hortensis / Satureja montana (summer and winter savory)

preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb infused and taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that savory warms the chest, helps bring up phlegm and ease a cough, expels wind, and comforts the stomach.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary herb, low-risk at food and tea strength for most people; the concentrated oil is a separate, stronger product, and medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary/traditional; little formal modern clinical evidence.

name: Devil's-bit Scabious
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root and herb boiled and the liquor taken, and applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that devil's-bit provokes sweat in fevers and 'pestilential' illness, helps the chest, and that a wash cleanses sores and skin eruptions.

modern_caution.notes: A mild traditional fever and skin herb, low-risk for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Water Germander (Scordium)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and it was a chief ingredient in old fever and 'plague' remedies.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that scordium provokes sweat and urine, was esteemed against fevers and infection, and helps to expel worms.

modern_caution.notes: Like other germanders (Teucrium), this plant is best treated with caution internally: related species have been linked to liver injury, so prolonged or heavy internal use is not advisable, and it is avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Historical fever/antidote use only; modern concern about liver toxicity across the Teucrium genus means internal use is not recommended without care.

name: Wood Sage
preparation_as_written: The text describes the bitter herb boiled and the liquor taken, and applied to wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that wood sage provokes urine and sweat, warms the stomach, and that a wash cleanses old sores and wounds.

modern_caution.notes: Another germander (Teucrium). Because plants in this genus have been linked to liver injury, prolonged or heavy internal use is best avoided, and it is not for use in pregnancy. External wound use is the lower-risk traditional application.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; the genus-wide liver-toxicity concern is the main reason to limit internal use.

name: Wall Germander
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and it featured in old remedies for gout and fevers.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that germander provokes urine and the courses, opens obstructions of the liver and spleen, and was used for gout and agues (fevers).

modern_caution.notes: Wall germander has been clearly linked to serious liver injury (hepatitis) in modern use — it was withdrawn as a slimming/weight-loss aid after causing cases of acute and sometimes fatal liver damage. It should not be taken internally, and it is also a traditional emmenagogue, so doubly unsuitable in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Modern evidence is firmly against internal use: documented hepatotoxicity led to its withdrawal from sale as a herbal product in several countries.

name: Red Poppy (Corn Poppy)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Papaver rhoeas (corn/field poppy) — NOT the opium poppy

preparation_as_written: The text describes the petals made into a syrup and a distilled water, and taken to ease the chest and bring rest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that the syrup of red poppy flowers eases coughs and helps to bring gentle rest and sleep.

modern_caution.notes: The corn poppy is much milder than the opium poppy and is not the same plant, but it still contains small amounts of active alkaloids. Home preparations have an unknown strength, and like all sedative remedies it should not be given to babies or young children, where poppy preparations have caused harm.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mild traditional sedative/cough use; limited modern evidence, and the caution about uncontrolled strength and children applies to all poppy preparations.

name: Clary
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb and seed used; a seed soaked to a mucilage was placed by the eye to draw out grit, and the herb taken in drinks.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that clary comforts the stomach and the back, and that the mucilage of the seed was used to clear the eye of dust and small specks.

modern_caution.notes: The herb and tea are low-risk for most people. The historical eye use is not advisable today — putting non-sterile material in the eye risks infection. Concentrated clary sage essential oil is a separate, stronger product.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional; little modern clinical evidence for the herb's internal uses.

name: Wild Lettuce

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Lactuca virosa (wild lettuce); garden lettuce, Lactuca sativa, was used similarly but more weakly

preparation_as_written: The text describes the milky juice ('lettuce opium') dried, and the herb boiled, taken to bring rest and ease pain.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that lettuce cools and brings sleep, eases pains, and quiets a hot, restless body.

modern_caution.notes: Wild lettuce's milky sap is a traditional mild sedative. It is much weaker than true opium, but large amounts of the concentrated sap can cause drowsiness, nausea, a fast heartbeat and dizziness, so it should not be combined with other sedatives or used in pregnancy, and home preparations have unknown strength.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional mild sedative/pain use; little reliable modern clinical evidence, and concentrated extracts can cause unwanted effects.

name: Shepherd's Purse
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the juice or liquor taken, and applied to stop bleeding.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that shepherd's purse strongly stays all kinds of bleeding — of wounds, nose, and the over-flowing of women's courses.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional remedy to slow bleeding, including heavy menstrual bleeding. Because it acts on the uterus and may affect blood pressure and clotting, it is avoided in pregnancy and by people on blood-pressure or blood-thinning medicines. Importantly, heavy or abnormal bleeding needs medical assessment rather than self-treatment.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Some traditional and limited modern use to reduce bleeding; evidence is weak, and the underlying cause of bleeding should be checked by a clinician.

name: Southernwood
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the bitter herb boiled and taken, and notes its use to 'bring down the courses' and to expel worms.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents southernwood to provoke women's courses, to kill and expel worms (especially in children), and to warm a cold stomach.

modern_caution.notes: Southernwood is a wormwood relative containing thujone, and is a traditional emmenagogue used to bring on periods. In those amounts it is toxic and must not be used in pregnancy (miscarriage risk) or for self-directed internal use; the worm-dosing of children with it is also unsafe.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use; the thujone toxicity and uterine-stimulant risks mean internal use is not recommended.

name: Lady's Mantle
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken and used as a wash.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that lady's mantle is binding, heals wounds and stays bleeding, and was much used as a strengthening herb for women.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent women's herb, low-risk as a tea for most people; as with other women's herbs, medicinal-strength use is best avoided in pregnancy, and abnormal bleeding should be checked by a clinician.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Columbine
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the leaves and seed used in drinks and gargles; the seed in particular was given in old recipes to ease childbirth.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents columbine for sore throats as a gargle, to help measles and smallpox come out, and the seed to ease and speed childbirth.

modern_caution.notes: Columbine, especially the seeds and roots, contains cyanide-forming compounds and is poisonous in more than tiny amounts — historical overdoses, including in attempts at the childbirth and other uses, caused serious poisoning. It is unsafe to take internally and must not be used in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe modern internal use; the plant is recognised as toxic, and there is no reliable evidence for the historical claims.

name: Burnet Saxifrage

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Pimpinella saxifraga (burnet saxifrage); 'saxifrage' covered several stone-breaking herbs

preparation_as_written: The text describes the root and herb boiled and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that saxifrage provokes urine, was used to break and expel the stone and gravel, and to ease wind.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional mild diuretic 'stone' herb, low-risk for most people. Note the historical name 'saxifrage' covered several different plants, so identity in old recipes is uncertain, and kidney-stone symptoms warrant medical assessment.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence, and the name covers more than one plant.

name: Gromwell
preparation_as_written: The text describes the hard, stony seeds powdered or boiled and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that gromwell provokes urine and was esteemed to break and drive out the stone and gravel and ease a stoppage of water.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional 'stone' herb (named for its stony seeds), low-risk for most people in occasional use. Kidney or bladder-stone symptoms should be medically assessed, and the related plant family can contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, so prolonged heavy use is best avoided.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional 'doctrine of signatures' use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Restharrow
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root boiled and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that restharrow provokes urine, opens a stoppage of water, and was used to break the stone.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional mild diuretic root, low-risk for most people. As with all diuretic herbs, it should be taken with enough fluids, and ongoing urinary symptoms need medical assessment.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Recognised as a mild traditional diuretic ('aquaretic') in some herbal pharmacopoeias; clinical evidence is limited.

name: Asparagus

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Asparagus officinalis (asparagus); the root was used medicinally

preparation_as_written: The text describes the root boiled and the liquor taken, and the young shoots eaten.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that asparagus root provokes urine, opens obstructions, and eases a stoppage of water and the stone.

modern_caution.notes: The shoots are a food and the root is a traditional mild diuretic, both low-risk for most people; take diuretic preparations with enough fluids, and check ongoing urinary or kidney symptoms with a clinician.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Recognised mild diuretic effect; the historical 'stone' claims are largely traditional.

name: Winter Cherry (Alkekengi)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Physalis alkekengi (bladder cherry/winter cherry) — not Withania somnifera, also called 'winter cherry'

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the ripe berries and their juice taken to provoke urine and drive out the stone.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents winter cherry to provoke urine strongly, to expel the stone and gravel, and to cleanse the kidneys and bladder.

modern_caution.notes: Only the fully ripe berry was traditionally used; the unripe fruit, leaves and the rest of the plant are toxic (containing bitter solanine-like compounds), and the plant has a traditional reputation as a uterine stimulant, so it must not be used in pregnancy. Given how easily the toxic parts are confused with the edible ripe berry, home use is not advisable.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Historical diuretic use only; the toxicity of the unripe fruit and other parts, and the pregnancy caution, make it unsuitable for home use.

name: Cinquefoil (Five-leaf Grass)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the astringent root and herb boiled and used as a gargle, wash and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that cinquefoil is binding, stays looseness and bleeding, and that a gargle of the decoction eases sore mouths, throats and loose gums.

modern_caution.notes: A tannin-rich astringent, low-risk as an occasional gargle or wash for most people; swallowing a lot of tannin can upset the stomach.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional astringent use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Red Rose

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Rosa gallica and related roses; the dried petals

preparation_as_written: The text describes the dried petals made into a binding syrup, conserve, honey and a distilled rose-water.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that red roses are gently binding and cooling, comfort the heart and stomach, and that rose preparations are used for sore mouths and throats.

modern_caution.notes: Rose petal preparations and rose water are mild and low-risk for most people. As with eyebright, home-made rose water is not sterile and is not suitable for putting in the eyes.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional and culinary; little formal modern clinical evidence.

name: Mulberry
preparation_as_written: The text describes the juice of the fruit made into a syrup, and the bark boiled, used as a gargle and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that mulberry syrup cools and eases a hot, sore mouth and throat, and that the bark was used against worms.

modern_caution.notes: The ripe fruit and its syrup are a food, low-risk for most people. Unripe mulberries can cause stomach upset, and the bark/root is stronger and less suitable for casual use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional and culinary; limited modern clinical evidence for the medicinal claims.

name: Privet
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the leaves boiled and used as a binding gargle and wash for the mouth and throat.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents a gargle of privet leaves for sore, ulcerated mouths and throats, and a wash for skin sores.

modern_caution.notes: Privet leaves and berries are poisonous if swallowed — the berries in particular have caused poisoning, especially in children. Even the traditional gargle use should be a gargle-and-spit only, never swallowed, and given the toxicity it is not a herb to use casually at home.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional external/gargle use only; the plant is recognised as toxic if ingested, with documented berry poisonings.

name: Mistletoe
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the berries and wood powdered or boiled and taken, especially as an old remedy for the 'falling sickness' (epilepsy).
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents mistletoe chiefly for the falling sickness (epilepsy) and convulsions, and applied to soften hard swellings.

modern_caution.notes: Raw mistletoe — leaves, stems and especially the white berries — is poisonous. Eating it can cause vomiting, a slowed or disturbed heartbeat, seizures and collapse, and children are particularly at risk from the berries. There is no safe home dose, and epilepsy or heart symptoms need proper medical care, not this plant.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Specially prepared, injectable mistletoe extracts are studied as an add-on in some cancer care under medical supervision, but the raw plant taken by mouth is toxic and unsafe for home use.

name: Wallflower
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the flowers made into a conserve and oil, and used in old remedies, including to 'provoke the courses'.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents wallflower preparations to provoke women's courses, to cleanse the womb, and an oil of the flowers to ease aches and dry, hard swellings.

modern_caution.notes: Wallflower seeds and plant contain heart-affecting compounds (cardiac glycosides) like those in foxglove, so internal use can dangerously disturb the heartbeat. It is also a traditional emmenagogue. It must not be taken internally, especially in pregnancy or by anyone with a heart condition.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Its cardiac glycosides are of historical pharmacological interest, but the plant has no safe home use and is potentially dangerous to the heart.

name: Coriander
preparation_as_written: The text describes the seed prepared (often coated in sugar as comfits) and taken after meals.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that prepared coriander seed helps wind and the gripings of the belly and settles the stomach after eating.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary spice, low-risk at food strength for most people. Culpeper himself warned against the raw green herb in quantity; the prepared seed is the gentle form.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional carminative; limited modern clinical evidence for mild digestive effects.

name: Cumin
preparation_as_written: The text describes the seed taken in food and drink, and made into a warming plaster for the belly.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that cumin expels wind, eases gripings and the cold pains of the belly, and that a plaster was laid on the stomach.

modern_caution.notes: A common culinary spice, low-risk at food strength for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional carminative use; some small modern studies on digestion, but evidence is limited.

name: Bay (Bay Laurel)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Laurus nobilis (bay laurel) — not the toxic ornamental cherry-laurel

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves used in cooking and the berries made into preparations, and an oil of the berries applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that bay warms and comforts a cold stomach, helps wind, and that the oil of the berries eases aches and bruises.

modern_caution.notes: Culinary bay leaves are low-risk used as flavouring (and removed before eating, as the stiff whole leaf can hurt the gut if swallowed). Do not confuse true bay with the poisonous ornamental cherry-laurel, whose leaves contain cyanide.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary/traditional; little formal modern clinical evidence.

name: Chervil

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Anthriscus cerefolium (garden chervil) — not to be confused with toxic hemlock-like umbellifers

preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb eaten in salads and broths and the juice taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that chervil warms and comforts the stomach, provokes urine, and that it was used to help bruises and clotted blood.

modern_caution.notes: A mild culinary herb, low-risk at food strength. The serious caution is identification: several deadly hemlock relatives resemble chervil, so only known cultivated chervil should be used.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary/traditional; little formal modern clinical evidence.

name: Alexanders
preparation_as_written: The text describes the stalks and roots eaten as a pot-herb and the seed used.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that alexanders warms the stomach, provokes urine and the courses, expels wind, and was eaten as a spring pot-herb.

modern_caution.notes: An old culinary pot-herb (a forerunner of celery), low-risk eaten in normal amounts; as with all wild umbellifers, correct identification away from poisonous relatives matters.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly historical culinary use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Succory (Chicory)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the bitter leaves and root boiled and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that succory cools a hot stomach and liver, opens obstructions, and was used for the jaundice and a feverish heat.

modern_caution.notes: A bitter salad and coffee-substitute plant, low-risk for most people; those allergic to the daisy family may react, and large amounts of the root are mildly laxative.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional bitter/liver use; the root (inulin) has some modern study as a prebiotic, but the historical claims are largely traditional.

name: Endive
preparation_as_written: The text describes the cooling leaves eaten and the juice or distilled water taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that endive cools and tempers a hot stomach and liver, quenches thirst in fevers, and helps the jaundice.

modern_caution.notes: A salad leaf, low-risk eaten in normal amounts for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary; the cooling/liver claims are traditional.

name: Dandelion
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves eaten and the root and herb boiled, the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that dandelion opens obstructions of the liver, provokes urine (hence its old name), and helps a feverish heat and the jaundice.

modern_caution.notes: A common edible plant and mild diuretic, low-risk for most people; those allergic to the daisy family may react, and its mild diuretic effect could add to water tablets.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional liver/diuretic use; limited modern clinical evidence, though a mild diuretic effect is plausible.

name: Polypody
preparation_as_written: The text describes the root boiled, often with other herbs, and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that polypody root gently purges tough phlegm and melancholy from the body and opens obstructions.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional gentle purging fern, low-risk in moderate amounts for most people; large amounts are mildly laxative and can upset the stomach.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Costmary (Alecost)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves used in ale and infusions and the herb taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that costmary warms and strengthens the stomach, helps digestion, and was used for the head and for women's complaints.

modern_caution.notes: Costmary is a relative of tansy and contains some thujone. Light culinary use of the leaf is mild, but it has a traditional emmenagogue (period-bringing) reputation and so is avoided in pregnancy, and strong or prolonged internal use is best avoided.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern evidence, and the thujone/pregnancy caution applies to strong use.

name: Dog's Mercury

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Mercurialis perennis (dog's mercury) — distinct from the milder annual 'French mercury' pot-herb

preparation_as_written: The historical text distinguishes this from the edible 'French mercury' and warns that dog's mercury is hurtful and not to be used as a pot-herb.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper notes dog's mercury chiefly to warn against it, contrasting it with the gentler garden mercury that was eaten and used as a mild purge.

modern_caution.notes: Dog's mercury is poisonous. It has caused serious and occasionally fatal poisoning when mistaken for an edible green and cooked — symptoms include vomiting, drowsiness and damage to the blood and kidneys. It is included here only because the source warns about it; it has no safe use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe use; recognised as a toxic plant with documented human poisonings, usually from misidentification as an edible herb.

name: Dwarf Elder (Danewort)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Sambucus ebulus (dwarf elder) — stronger and more toxic than common elder

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the root, leaves and berries boiled and taken as a strong purge and to draw off watery humours.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents dwarf elder as a powerful purge for dropsy (fluid swelling) and to expel watery and 'gross' humours, and applied to swellings and gout.

modern_caution.notes: Dwarf elder is much stronger and more toxic than common elder. It is a drastic purgative, and the raw plant and berries can cause violent vomiting, diarrhoea and poisoning. It is unsafe for self-directed use and must not be confused with the milder common elder.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Historical drastic-purgative use only; the plant is recognised as toxic and is not recommended for home use.

name: Spignel (Baldmoney)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the aromatic root boiled and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that spignel warms the stomach, helps wind and the gripings of the belly, and provokes urine.

modern_caution.notes: An aromatic root traditionally used like other warming carminatives, low-risk in moderate amounts; as with all umbellifers, correct identification matters.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Samphire
preparation_as_written: The text describes the fleshy leaves pickled and eaten, and used in the diet.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that samphire opens obstructions, provokes urine and appetite, and helps digestion as a wholesome pickle.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional edible coastal plant, low-risk eaten in normal amounts.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary; little specific modern medical evidence.

name: Rocket
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves eaten in salads and the seed used.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that rocket warms the stomach, provokes appetite and urine, and helps digestion, advising it be eaten with cooling leaves.

modern_caution.notes: A common salad leaf, low-risk eaten in normal amounts; very large pungent amounts can irritate a sensitive stomach.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly culinary; little specific modern medical evidence for the historical claims.

name: Purslane
preparation_as_written: The text describes the cooling, juicy leaves eaten in salads and the juice taken, and applied to the skin.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that purslane cools a hot stomach and a feverish heat, quenches thirst, and that the leaves were laid on hot, inflamed skin and eased a hot, sore mouth.

modern_caution.notes: An edible succulent leaf, low-risk eaten in normal amounts; it is fairly high in oxalates, so very large quantities are best avoided by people prone to kidney stones.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Nutritious leafy plant (a source of omega-3s); the historical cooling claims are traditional.

name: Hart's Tongue
preparation_as_written: The text describes the fern boiled in water or wine and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that hart's tongue opens obstructions of the liver and spleen, stays looseness and bleeding, and was used for a hot, feverish liver.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent traditional liver/spleen herb, low-risk in moderate amounts for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Catmint (Nep)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and made into a poultice.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that catmint warms the stomach, eases wind and the gripings of the belly, provokes the courses, and was used to bring on sweat in colds.

modern_caution.notes: A mild traditional tea herb (the one cats love), low-risk for most people at tea strength; because of its traditional period-bringing use, medicinal-strength amounts are best avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Mostly traditional use for mild digestive and calming effects; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Adder's Tongue
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb made into a green ointment ('green oil') and applied to wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that an ointment of adder's tongue heals green wounds, eases inflammations, and is good for sore eyes and bruises.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional wound-ointment herb, low-risk applied to minor, clean skin for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Bugle
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb bruised and applied, and boiled into a wound-drink and wash.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that bugle heals wounds and ulcers inward and outward, stays bleeding, and was esteemed for bruises and falls.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional wound herb, low-risk for most people on minor, clean wounds.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; limited modern evidence.

name: Lady's Bedstraw
preparation_as_written: The text describes the flowering herb boiled and used as a wash and bath, and made into an ointment.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that lady's bedstraw stays bleeding, heals burns and skin sores, and that a bath of it eases tired, aching feet.

modern_caution.notes: A mild traditional skin and foot-bath herb, low-risk for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Daisy
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb bruised and applied, and boiled into a wound-drink and ointment.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that daisies ease and heal bruises, wounds and swellings, and that a drink of them was used for inward hurts and falls.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional bruise-and-wound herb, low-risk for most people on minor injuries; those allergic to the daisy family may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Toadflax
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled into a wash and ointment and the juice applied, and a decoction taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that toadflax provokes urine, opens obstructions, and that an ointment of it eases piles and stubborn, inflamed skin sores.

modern_caution.notes: Used mainly on the skin and traditionally low-risk there; internal use in large amounts can be mildly purgative and diuretic, so it is best kept to occasional use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Moneywort (Creeping Jenny)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb bruised and applied, and boiled into a wash and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that moneywort heals wounds, stays bleeding and fluxes, and that a wash cleanses sores and skin eruptions.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional wound and skin herb, low-risk for most people on minor complaints.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Loosestrife (Yellow Loosestrife)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and used as a wash, gargle and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that loosestrife stays bleeding and fluxes, cleanses and heals wounds, and that a gargle helps sore mouths.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional astringent wound and gargle herb, low-risk for most people in moderate use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Pilewort (Lesser Celandine)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Ficaria verna (lesser celandine), formerly Ranunculus ficaria — unrelated to the greater celandine

preparation_as_written: The text describes the root and herb made into an ointment and applied, chiefly for piles.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that pilewort, named for the purpose, was used as an ointment and bath to ease and shrink piles (haemorrhoids).

modern_caution.notes: The fresh plant is acrid and irritating (it contains protoanemonin), and should not be used raw or taken internally — it can blister skin and irritate the gut. Traditionally it was dried or made into ointment, which tames it, and even then it is for external use only.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional external use for piles; the fresh plant's irritant toxicity is well recognised, so only dried/processed external preparations were used.

name: Bittersweet (Woody Nightshade)
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the twigs and stalks boiled and the liquor taken, and applied to the skin, for stubborn complaints.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents bittersweet for stubborn skin eruptions, swellings and bruises, and was used inwardly for rheumatic and feverish complaints.

modern_caution.notes: Woody nightshade is a poisonous member of the nightshade family. Its leaves, stems and especially the bright red berries contain solanine-type toxins that cause vomiting, drowsiness, a slowed heartbeat and, in larger amounts, collapse; children have been poisoned by the attractive berries. It is unsafe for internal home use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe internal home use; the plant is recognised as toxic, with documented poisonings, especially in children from the berries.

name: Tutsan

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Hypericum androsaemum (tutsan); a relative of St John's wort

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves made into an oil and ointment and laid on wounds and burns.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that tutsan heals wounds and burns, eases bruises, and that the leaves were laid on broken skin.

modern_caution.notes: Used mainly as a wound-and-burn ointment and traditionally low-risk on the skin. As a relative of St John's wort it can increase sensitivity to sunlight, so treated skin is best kept out of strong sun.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional skin use; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Herb Robert
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb bruised and applied, and boiled into a wash and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that herb Robert stays bleeding, heals wounds and old ulcers, and was used as a wash for sore skin.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional astringent wound herb, low-risk for most people on minor complaints.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Mouse-ear
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken and used as a wash.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that mouse-ear stays bleeding and fluxes, heals wounds inward and outward, and was used for a cough and the chest.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent traditional herb, low-risk for most people; those allergic to the daisy family may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Ivy
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the leaves boiled and used as a wash and the berries and gum used, applied to the skin and taken with caution.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents ivy applied to running sores and the skin, and the leaves used about the head and chest, while the plant was always treated as sharp and not wholly safe.

modern_caution.notes: A standardised ivy-leaf extract is used in modern cough medicines, but the raw plant is different: ivy leaves and berries contain irritant saponins, the berries are toxic if eaten (a risk to children), and the sap commonly causes skin rashes. Home preparations of raw ivy are not safe to swallow.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Standardised ivy-leaf cough preparations have reasonable modern evidence, but that is a controlled extract — the raw plant carries irritant and toxicity risks.

name: Cudweed
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and used as a gargle and drink.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that cudweed is binding, stays looseness and bleeding, and that a gargle helps quinsy and sore, relaxed throats.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent gargle herb, low-risk for most people in occasional use.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Hedge Mustard

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Sisymbrium officinale (hedge mustard); long called 'the singer's plant'

preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled, often with honey, and the liquor or syrup taken for the throat and chest.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that hedge mustard helps hoarseness and the loss of voice, and clears the chest and throat of tough phlegm.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional throat-and-voice herb, low-risk as a tea or syrup for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional use for hoarseness ('the singer's plant'); modern clinical evidence is limited.

name: Pellitory of Spain

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Anacyclus pyrethrum (pellitory of Spain) root — distinct from pellitory-of-the-wall

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the hot, biting root chewed or held in the mouth to draw water and rheum from the head and ease toothache.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents pellitory of Spain chewed to ease toothache and to draw 'rheum' from the head, and used for a palsied tongue.

modern_caution.notes: An intensely acrid root that makes the mouth burn and stream with saliva. Used briefly in the mouth and spat out it is a traditional toothache remedy, but it is a strong irritant: it should not be swallowed in quantity, and a toothache really needs a dentist.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Traditional local irritant/saliva-promoting use; little modern clinical evidence, and dental causes need proper treatment.

name: Bilberry (Whortleberry)
preparation_as_written: The text describes the berries eaten and made into a binding syrup or conserve.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that bilberries cool a hot stomach, stay looseness and bleeding, and that the syrup eases a hot, sore mouth and throat.

modern_caution.notes: The berries are a food, and dried-berry preparations are a low-risk traditional remedy for mild looseness for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Dried bilberry has some modern recognition for short-term mild diarrhoea; the fruit is a well-regarded food.

name: Burnet (Salad Burnet)

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Sanguisorba minor (salad burnet) and Sanguisorba officinalis (great burnet)

preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves used in cooling drinks and salads, and boiled into a wound-drink and wash.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that burnet cheers the heart in fevers, stays bleeding and looseness, and that it heals wounds inward and outward.

modern_caution.notes: A mild salad and astringent herb, low-risk for most people.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence for the medicinal claims.

name: Scarlet Pimpernel

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Lysimachia arvensis (scarlet pimpernel), formerly Anagallis arvensis

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and the juice applied to wounds and to draw out splinters.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents pimpernel to cheer the spirits, against infection and the bites of venomous creatures, and applied to draw out thorns and cleanse wounds.

modern_caution.notes: Scarlet pimpernel contains irritant saponins and is toxic in more than small amounts — it can irritate the gut and kidneys and cause skin rashes on contact. Internal home use is not advisable, and it is avoided in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Historical use only; the plant is recognised as potentially toxic, so internal use is discouraged.

name: Goat's Rue
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, used in fevers and to expel poison.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that goat's rue provokes sweat, was used against fevers, pestilence and the bites of venomous creatures, and to expel worms.

modern_caution.notes: Goat's rue lowers blood sugar (its compound galegine inspired the diabetes drug metformin), so it can interact with diabetes medicines and cause low blood sugar. The plant is also toxic to grazing animals in quantity. It should not be used casually, especially by people on blood-sugar medication or who are pregnant.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Of historical interest as a blood-sugar-lowering plant and traditional galactagogue; the blood-sugar interaction is the main modern caution and self-use is not advised.

name: Fleabane
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and burned to drive away fleas and gnats.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that fleabane was used to stay looseness (especially the bloody flux), and burned to drive away biting insects.

modern_caution.notes: A mild astringent traditional herb, low-risk in occasional use for most people; those allergic to the daisy family may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Dittany

ingredients.modern_equivalent: Dictamnus albus (white dittany/burning bush) and the related 'dittany of Crete', Origanum dictamnus

preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb taken in drinks and notes its old reputation to 'bring away the birth' and provoke the courses.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents dittany to provoke women's courses, to hasten delivery and bring away the afterbirth or dead child, and against poisons.

modern_caution.notes: Dittany has a long reputation as a herb to bring on menstruation and expel a pregnancy, which makes self-directed use dangerous. White dittany also contains furocoumarins that cause severe sun-triggered skin burns on contact. It must not be used in pregnancy or for self-directed internal use; a missed period or pregnancy concern is a matter for a clinician.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: No safe modern internal use for the historical purposes; the emmenagogue reputation and phototoxicity make it unsuitable for home use.

name: Madder
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the root boiled and the liquor taken, noting that it colours the urine red.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents madder to provoke urine and the courses, to open obstructions of the liver and spleen, and for bruises and the jaundice.

modern_caution.notes: Beyond harmlessly turning urine (and historically teeth and bones) red, madder root contains compounds (such as lucidin) now shown to damage genetic material and to be potentially cancer-causing — which is why madder-root supplements have been withdrawn from sale in several countries. It is also a traditional emmenagogue. It should not be taken internally, and especially not in pregnancy.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Modern evidence is against internal use: genotoxic/carcinogenic constituents led to madder-root products being banned or withdrawn in several countries.

name: Parsley Piert
preparation_as_written: The text describes the small herb boiled and the liquor taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that parsley piert provokes urine and was much esteemed to break and expel the stone and gravel and ease a stoppage of water.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional mild diuretic 'stone' herb, low-risk for most people; take with enough fluids, and have ongoing kidney or bladder symptoms checked by a clinician.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Largely traditional; little modern clinical evidence.

name: Birch
preparation_as_written: The text describes the leaves boiled and the spring sap drawn off and taken.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that birch leaves and sap provoke urine, were used to break the stone, and that the sap was a spring cleansing drink.

modern_caution.notes: Birch-leaf tea and sap are mild traditional diuretics, low-risk for most people; take with enough fluids. People allergic to birch pollen may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Birch leaf is a recognised mild traditional diuretic ('aquaretic') in some herbal pharmacopoeias; clinical evidence is limited.

name: Golden Rod
preparation_as_written: The text describes the herb boiled and the liquor taken, and used as a wash for wounds.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper writes that golden rod provokes urine, was esteemed to break the stone and heal the kidneys, and that a wash cleansed wounds and sores.

modern_caution.notes: A traditional diuretic and wound herb, low-risk for most people; take diuretic preparations with enough fluids. Those allergic to the daisy family may react.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: Golden rod is a recognised mild traditional diuretic for urinary 'flushing' in some herbal pharmacopoeias; clinical evidence is modest.

name: Viper's Bugloss
preparation_as_written: The historical text describes the herb and root boiled in wine and taken as a cordial.
symptoms_addressed_as_written: Culpeper presents viper's bugloss as a cordial to comfort the heart and drive away melancholy, against fevers and poison, and to ease the bites of venomous creatures.

modern_caution.notes: Like borage and comfrey, viper's bugloss contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can cause serious liver damage, particularly with repeated use. Taking it internally is now considered unsafe, and it should not be used in pregnancy or by children.
modern_caution.modern_evidence_status: The traditional 'cordial' use is unsupported by good evidence, and the liver-toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids mean internal use is not recommended.
